questions.q: How many correct uses of the apostrophe does Truss list?
a: Eight
Five
Seven
Ten
questions.why: Lesson 1 says there are essentially only eight correct ways to use the apostrophe, from possessives to omitted letters.

questions.q: How many comma rules does the author highlight?
a: Seven
Four
Eight
Ten
questions.why: Lesson 2 lists seven rules for using commas, from enumerating lists to bracketing weak interruptions.

questions.q: What does Truss compare a language to?
a: A living organism that grows and changes
A machine that needs careful maintenance
A building constructed from firm rules
A game with fixed and unbreakable rules
questions.why: Lesson 1 opens by describing language as a living organism that develops, twists and changes over time.

questions.q: What does she recommend instead of piling on exclamation marks?
a: Use periods and plain words to carry the feeling
Use capitals to emphasize the important words
Add quotation marks around emotional phrases
Write longer sentences to explain the emotion
questions.why: Lesson 3 says to embrace the period and use words to convey sentiment rather than relying on punctuation.

questions.q: What does Truss say makes a text easier to digest?
a: Cutting it into bite-size chunks and avoiding long sentences
Adding commas wherever a pause feels natural
Using more question marks to engage the reader
Keeping every paragraph to a single idea
questions.why: Lesson 3 recommends cutting text into bite-size chunks so the audience can digest it more easily.
